title: Walk Time: How safe are we?
summary:
By Robert Niles: A discussion on Theme Park Insider's forum sums up what many fans are wondering this week, How safe are we?

Six Flags theme parks on Friday posted messages from their park presidents to their social media accounts. Each message said, "Our guests and team members are what make this park so special, and their safety will always be our highest priority. We remain committed to making safety the focus of everything we do, every day. We can�t wait to see you this weekend."

And just hours after posting that message, Cedar Point had to close Millennium Force when a metal bracket fell off the ride. Remember that a part flying off a coaster is what did in the original Top Thrill Dragster. Those were both Intamin rides, not Bolliger & Mabillard, which is the manufacturer of the Goliath ride at Six Flags Over Georgia that kicked off this latest round of industry angst when a 42-year-old died on the last turn of the coaster due to what appears to be a restraint failure.

What fans need from Six Flags management is not a platitude about safety. We need transparency about the investigation into the Goliath incident. What is the plan for and progress of that investigation? No reasonable person expects immediate answers. Fans want investigators to take all the time needed to do their job right. But that does not prevent the company from sharing information about who will be doing the investigation and what they will be examining.

Jake and I talked more about this in this week's Theme Park Insider Podcast episode, Processing the Six Flags Goliath tragedy.

Meanwhile, the company's debt remains in the billions and its stock price is down to $8.11 - down 67% from its 2026 high of $24.94 on June 19. The stock was trading over $57 a share when the Cedar Fair merger closed in 2024. Looks like that deal worked out for everyone, huh? /s

Following all this, I have revived our Accident Watch page, documenting fatal injury accidents at U.S. theme parks since Theme Park Insider's founding in 2000.

Interest note: Of the 29 fatalities listed on that page now, 13 claimed park employees. That's 45% - much higher than I expected. Moreover, stories about guest victims include results such as $200 million-plus court judgments against the parks. But the employee deaths include notes such as $11,000 OSHA fines. As a former theme park employee, it's depressing to see how little we value the lives of workers in this country.

I will post some additional week in review notes in tomorrow's "Rope Drop" weekly preview. Until then, stay safe, and thank a theme park employee.

title: Disneyland character performers to rally for labor deal
summary:
By Robert Niles: Disneyland cast members are planning a rally near the park's entrance tomorrow morning, as they seek a new labor contract with Disney.

The "Rally for a Fair Contract" starts at 10am on Saturday, October 17, on the northwest corner of Harbor Blvd. and W. Katella Ave. (That's the corner with the 7-11.) Two years ago, 1,700 Disneyland cast members in the Characters and Parades departments voted to form a union with the Actors' Equity Association. However, they still don't have a deal with Disney, and union leaders accuse the company of slow-walking negotiations.

"The message you will hear at our rally is that despite Disney�s actions to date, we remain willing and able to bargain with the company to reach a fair contract for the character and parades workers who are the public face of Disneyland and who make a visit to the park rewarding," Equity Executive Director Al Vincent Jr. said.

Most of the rest of Disneyland's workforce is unionized and have their own deals with the company. Unions also represent character performers at the Walt Disney World Resort in Florida.

Actors' Equity Association was founded in 1913 and is the major union representing 51,000 professional stage actors and stage managers across the country, including Broadway.

title: Record-setting wing coaster set for 2027 debut
summary:
By Robert Niles: The world's number-one coaster park is adding a record-setting wing coaster for next year.

Energylandia has announced Rokan, a Bolliger & Mabillard wing coaster, which will be the 20th roller coaster at the Polish theme park. That's the current world record for most coasters at one park.

Rokan will be 203 feet tall, making it the tallest B & M wing coaster in the world. For comparison, Rapterra at Kings Dominion in the U.S. is just 145 feet tall.

Unlike Rapterra, Rokan will have a chain lift hill rather than a launch, but the coaster will reach a top speed of 71.5 mph, which is faster than Rapterra's 65 mph. Riders will experience four inversions along Rokan's 3,986-foot track.


Rokan track. Rendering courtesy Energylandia

Here is the hype video from the park.

title: Universal details new radar system for guest safety
summary:
By Robert Niles: Universal has plans for using a new tool to detect when guests go someplace that they shouldn't in a theme park.

Theme parks long have used a variety of ways to keep guests out of restricted areas. Walls and fences provide hard barriers to backstage and secured locations. For especially sensitive areas, such as ride tracks and equipment rooms, parks also use monitoring devices to restrict guests access.

Some of those devices include intrusion mats, IR beams and camera monitoring systems. Now, Universal is proposing a way to use radar to monitor and restrict guest access to designated areas.

Universal describes its plans in a new patent application published today, System and Method for Detecting Guests in Restricted Areas. In its application, Universal notes the problems with many existing intrusion detection systems.

"These systems often do not provide sufficient early detection or warning, potentially resulting in the guest disembarking from the ride vehicle before the systems can take action to stop the ride vehicle or otherwise protect the guest's safety. Therefore, an inexpensive and simple system and a method which can detect if a guest is attempting to engage in unsafe activities or disembark a ride vehicle before the guest does so would be useful."

Universal's system uses one or more radar devices to monitor ride vehicles and restricted areas.

In one example, "the computing system is programmed to detect whether there is a breach in at least the first radar field or the second radar field and adjust an operation of the ride vehicle when the breach is detected," Universal's patent application states.

You can read the entire application on the US Patent and Trademark Office's website.

title: Processing the Six Flags Goliath tragedy
summary:
By Robert Niles: This week on the Theme Park Insider Podcast, Jake and I talk about what Six Flags needs to do to respect the memory of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, by finding out what led to his death on the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia and sharing the results of that investigation with the public.

Following this week's incident, I have revived Theme Park Insider's Accident Watch page. This is no longer a crowd-sourced list of accident reports, as the emergence of bots and automated agents made policing that a task I was no longer willing to handle. The page now lists our coverage of fatal injury accidents at U.S. theme parks since the site began in 2000.

It's an ongoing project as I backfill links onto the page, so please let me know about incidents that I have missed. I am including only fatalities due to injury incidents at this time and not deaths that are wholly the result of pre-existing health conditions.

title: Dollywood sets 2027 calendar, opening date
summary:
By Robert Niles: Dollywood will open for the 2027 season on March 11, the park announced today.

Next year will be the first full season for the Pigeon Forge, Tennessee park's new NightFlight Expedition ride. It also will be the first season opening at the park since the passing of co-founder and "Dreamer in Chief" Dolly Parton.

The park will honor Dolly next year with the debut of a new character, the Dream Maker, in the Wildwood Grove area.

"The Dream Maker and her Dream Wagon will give children an opportunity to share their own dreams, hear stories inspired by Dolly and discover that dreams can become even more meaningful when they are shared with others," the park said of this addition.

Also honoring Dolly, the park kicks of its 2027 season with the return of the I Will Always Love You Music Festival, which runs through April 11. "From the Heart � The Life & Music of Dolly Parton" show will return this year for the festival, running in Celebrity Theater through the end of the Flower & Food Festival in June.

Here are other announced events on Dollywood's 2027 calendar:

  • April 23-25: Run Dollywood spring event
  • May 7 - June 20: Dollywood's Flower & Food Festival
  • June 26 - Aug. 8: Dollywood's Smoky Mountain Summer Celebration
  • Sept. 3-6: Dollywood's Barbeque & Bluegrass
  • Sept. 11 - Oct. 31: Dollywood's Harvest Festival
  • Sept. 24-26: Run Dollywood fall event
  • Oct. 1, 15, 22, 23, 29 and 30: Harvey's Boo Bash at Dollywood
  • Nov. 5 - Jan. 2, 2028: Dollywood's Smoky Mountain Christmas
  • Nov. 12-14: Run Dollywood Christmas event

Dollywood's season concludes with the end of the Smoky Mountain Christmas event.

Season passes for 2027 will go on sale Monday, Nov. 2 on Dollywood's website.

title: Disney reveals name for its final Wish-class ship, in Japan
summary:
By Robert Niles: We now know the name of Disney's final Wish-class cruise ship.

Last week, Disney Cruise Line revealed details about Disney Believe, the fourth Wish-class ship, which is set to sail from Fort Lauderdale beginning in December 2027. After that, Disney had planned a fifth and final Wish-class ship, to be owned and operated by Oriental Land Co., the company behind the Tokyo Disney Resort.

Today, Disney and OLC announced that ship will be named Disney Imagination. It will begin sailing from Tokyo International Cruise Terminal in spring 2029.

The Little Mermaid, Ariel, will be the stern character for the ship, which will operate under the OLC's new Disney Cruise Line Japan business.


Image courtesy Oriental Land Co.

Like the other Wish-class ships, Disney Imagination will include three main dining restaurants and a 1,300-seat main theater, as well as bars, cafes, deck shows, children's programs, and character meets. However, OLC did not confirm any specific themes or programs for its ship.

So I guess that Disney Cruise fans can hold hope that maybe this ship won't include a Worlds of Marvel?

Of course, with OLC running the show, it is not yet clear whether Castaway Club will be a thing on Disney Imagination, or whether OLC will have its own loyalty program. That would affect booking priority and access to programs and locations on the ship, which are often determined by Castaway Club status on DCL ships.

Those details, as well as information about specific itineraries and sail dates, will be coming at some future date.

After the completion of the Wish class, Disney Cruise Line has announced plans for three more ships in a new, smaller class, to set sail between 2029 and 2030.

title: What really happened on Six Flags' Goliath coaster?
summary:
By Robert Niles: It's hard for me to think about much other than yesterday's terrible accident at Six Flags Over Georgia. So let's get into what we know - and need to know - about the death of a rider on the park's Goliath roller coaster.

Multiple reports have identified the victim as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, an Atlanta school IT worker. I can't imagine what his family or others who were on the ride are going through right now. But I am certain that the entire coaster fan community is grieving along with them. Moving forward, I hope that the family finds the peace that they need.

For the rest of us, we need answers. What, exactly, happened here and what caused that to happen? Local authorities are investigating, joined by representative from the coaster's manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard. As a fan and coaster rider, I want to know if something failed here, and if so, how and why.

Knowing what I know about roller coaster design and physics, it seems incomprehensible to me that a restraint would fail at an ejector airtime moment and that the ride's momentum design would allow that failure to result in a rider being ejected from their seat with enough force to strike and injure others on the train before falling clear of the train. Yet that is what witnesses on the train have described, according to multiple professional news media reports.

Only a well-investigated, detailed explanation of the incident can provide the guidance that the industry will confirm what happened and to help prevent the result of this incident from happening again. But that information will not help reassure an anxious public if those findings are not shared with them.

Transparency is essential. On that point, Six Flags' short-term and long-term business interests diverge.

Obviously, any news stories or announcements about the investigation should respect the victim's family and their loss. But the public will need to hear the results of this investigation, as painful as those results might be to hear for those closest to the incident.

In the near term, I imagine that Six Flags would be happy for this story to fade from public attention and for it to be able to reopen its B & M hyper coasters for fans who do not care about what happened in Georgia. But Six Flags - and the industry - over the long term needs the public to believe that all of its thrill rides are safe. We need to know that what happened on Goliath does not represent some flaw or malpractice that could result in a similar failure on another coaster, whether it be a B & M hyper or other model.

That means Six Flags needs to get out in front of the news and provide updates about the investigation, rather than waiting until the outcry of questions becomes so loud than no answers will be heard.

Six Flags waited way too long to address concerns about its X2 coaster at Magic Mountain. That reticence spent Six Flags' goodwill down to zero. The company cannot afford to mishandle its response to the Georgia death.

Some within the company might argue that silence is the appropriate response. For the moment, perhaps. But very soon, we should hear from the company about its plans for this investigation and the release of its findings.

Six Flags' stock price dropped 14% today. This story should not be about money, but money matters. Six Flags was already straining under pandemic-era debt. Litigation over X2 could mean additional financial burden for the company. Now, Six Flags is facing whatever costs and lost income that might result from the Georgia incident.

This is a dark moment for Six Flags. The company needs leadership that can light a path forward through all of the company's challenges.
